questions.prompt: Explain what inheritance is in Swift, which types support it, and what base classes are.

rubric.criterion: Explains that inheritance allows a subclass to inherit methods and properties from a superclass
States clearly that only classes support inheritance in Swift
Notes that Swift does not have a universal base class and any class without a superclass is a base class

questions.modelAnswer: Inheritance allows a subclass to inherit stored properties, computed properties, and methods from a superclass. In Swift, only classes support inheritance; structs and enumerations cannot inherit. Swift does not have a universal root object like NSObject. Any class without an explicit superclass is an independent base class.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require the override keyword when overriding methods or properties, and how can code call the superclass version?

rubric.criterion: Explains that the override keyword allows the compiler to check that a matching declaration exists in the superclass
Explains that code can call the superclass implementation using the super keyword (like super.methodName())

questions.modelAnswer: Swift requires the override keyword so the compiler can verify that a matching method or property exists in the superclass. This prevents accidental spelling or parameter mismatches. Inside an overridden method or property, you can call the superclass implementation using the super keyword, such as super.methodName().

questions.prompt: What does the final modifier do when applied to a class or a method, and how does it benefit performance?

rubric.criterion: Explains that final prevents classes from being subclassed and prevents methods from being overridden
Explains that final allows the compiler to use direct static dispatch instead of dynamic table dispatch

questions.modelAnswer: The final keyword prevents a class from being subclassed or a method from being overridden. Because the compiler knows no overrides can exist, it replaces dynamic table dispatch with fast direct static dispatch. This improves runtime performance and enables compiler inlining optimizations.

questions.prompt: What is the two-phase initialization rule in Swift subclassing, and why must subclass properties be initialized before calling super.init()?

rubric.criterion: Explains that in Phase 1, the subclass must initialize all of its own new stored properties before delegating up to super.init()
Explains that in Phase 2, after super.init() finishes, self can be referenced and properties can be customized
Mentions that this prevents uninitialized memory access before superclass initializers execute

questions.modelAnswer: Swift enforces two-phase initialization to prevent accessing memory before it is initialized. In Phase 1, the subclass must assign initial values to all its new stored properties before calling super.init(). In Phase 2, once super.init() returns, the instance is fully initialized, allowing self to be referenced and methods to be called.

questions.prompt: Why do Swift architects recommend composition and protocol-oriented programming over deep class inheritance hierarchies?

rubric.criterion: Explains that deep inheritance causes tight coupling and fragile base class problems
Explains that composition and protocols allow decoupled, modular reuse across both value types and reference types
States that value types avoid shared mutable state and retain cycle risks

questions.modelAnswer: Deep inheritance hierarchies create tight coupling and fragile base classes, where small parent changes break subclasses unexpectedly. Composition and protocols allow decoupled reuse across both structs and classes. Using value types with protocols avoids reference sharing, retain cycles, and unintended side effects.
